{{Short description|Term in stochastic calculus}}

In [[stochastic calculus]], '''stochastic logarithm''' of a [[semimartingale]] <math>Y</math>such that <math>Y\neq0</math> and <math>Y_-\neq0</math> is the semimartingale <math>X</math> given by<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last1=Jacod|first1=Jean|title=Limit theorems for stochastic processes|last2=Shiryaev|first2=Albert Nikolaevich|date=2003|publisher=Springer|isbn=3-540-43932-3|edition=2nd|location=Berlin|pages=134–138|oclc=50554399}}</ref><math display="block">dX_t=\frac{dY_t}{Y_{t-}},\quad X_0=0.</math>In layperson's terms, stochastic logarithm of  <math>Y</math> measures the cumulative percentage change in <math>Y</math>.

== Notation and terminology ==
The process <math>X</math> obtained above is commonly denoted <math>\mathcal{L}(Y)</math>. The terminology ''stochastic logarithm'' arises from the similarity of <math>\mathcal{L}(Y)</math> to the [[natural logarithm]] <math>\log(Y)</math>: If <math>Y</math> is absolutely continuous with respect to time and <math>Y\neq 0</math>, then ''<math>X</math>'' solves, path-by-path, the [[differential equation]] <math display="block">\frac{dX_t}{dt} = \frac{\frac{dY_t}{dt}}{Y_t},</math>whose solution is <math>X =\log|Y|-\log|Y_0|</math>. 

== General formula and special cases ==

* Without any assumptions on the semimartingale <math>Y</math> (other than <math>Y\neq 0, Y_-\neq 0</math>), one has<ref name=":1" /><math display="block">\mathcal{L}(Y)_t = \log\Biggl|\frac{Y_t}{Y_0}\Biggl|
+\frac12\int_0^t\frac{d[Y]^c_s}{Y_{s-}^2}
+\sum_{s\le t}\Biggl(\log\Biggl| 1 + \frac{\Delta Y_s}{Y_{s-}} \Biggr|
-\frac{\Delta Y_s}{Y_{s-}}\Biggr),\qquad t\ge0,</math>where <math>[Y]^c</math> is the continuous part of [[quadratic variation]] of <math>Y</math> and the sum extends over the (countably many) jumps of <math>Y</math> up to time <math>t</math>.
* If <math>Y</math> is continuous, then <math display="block">\mathcal{L}(Y)_t = \log\Biggl|\frac{Y_t}{Y_0}\Biggl|
+\frac12\int_0^t\frac{d[Y]^c_s}{Y_{s-}^2},\qquad t\ge0.</math>In particular, if <math>Y</math> is a [[geometric Brownian motion]], then <math>X</math> is a Brownian motion with a constant drift rate.
* If <math>Y</math> is continuous and of finite variation, then<math display="block">\mathcal{L}(Y) = \log\Biggl|\frac{Y}{Y_0}\Biggl|.</math>Here <math>Y</math> need not be differentiable with respect to time; for example, <math>Y</math> can equal 1 plus the [[Cantor function]].

== Properties ==

* Stochastic logarithm is an inverse operation to [[Doléans-Dade exponential|stochastic exponential]]: If <math>\Delta X\neq -1</math>, then <math>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{E}(X)) = X-X_0</math>. Conversely, if <math>Y\neq 0</math>  and <math>Y_-\neq 0</math>, then <math>\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{L}(Y)) = Y/Y_0</math>.<ref name=":1" />
* Unlike the natural logarithm <math>\log(Y_t)</math>, which depends only of the value of <math>Y</math> at time <math>t</math>, the stochastic logarithm <math>\mathcal{L}(Y)_t</math> depends not only on <math>Y_t</math> but on the whole history of <math>Y</math> in the time interval <math>[0,t]</math>. For this reason one must write <math>\mathcal{L}(Y)_t</math> and not <math>\mathcal{L}(Y_t)</math>.
* Stochastic logarithm of a [[local martingale]] that does not vanish together with its left limit  is again a local martingale.
* All the formulae and properties above apply also to stochastic logarithm of a [[Complex number|complex]]-valued <math>Y</math>.
* Stochastic logarithm can be defined also for processes <math>Y</math> that are absorbed in zero after jumping to zero. Such definition is meaningful up to the first time that  <math>Y</math> reaches <math>0</math> continuously.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Larsson|first1=Martin|last2=Ruf|first2=Johannes|date=2019|title=Stochastic exponentials and logarithms on stochastic intervals — A survey|journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications|language=en|volume=476|issue=1|pages=2–12|doi=10.1016/j.jmaa.2018.11.040|s2cid=119148331 |doi-access=free|arxiv=1702.03573}}</ref>

== Useful identities ==

* Converse of the Yor formula:<ref name=":1" /> If <math>Y^{(1)},Y^{(2)}</math> do not vanish together with their left limits, then<math display="block">\mathcal{L}\bigl(Y^{(1)}Y^{(2)}\bigr) = \mathcal{L}\bigl(Y^{(1)}\bigr) 
+ \mathcal{L}\bigl(Y^{(2)}\bigr) 
+ \bigl[\mathcal{L}\bigl(Y^{(1)}\bigr),\mathcal{L}\bigl(Y^{(2)}\bigr)\bigr].</math>
* Stochastic logarithm of <math>1/\mathcal{E}(X)</math>:<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Larsson|first1=Martin|last2=Ruf|first2=Johannes|date=2019|title=Stochastic exponentials and logarithms on stochastic intervals — A survey|journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications|language=en|volume=476|issue=1|pages=2–12|doi=10.1016/j.jmaa.2018.11.040|s2cid=119148331 |doi-access=free|arxiv=1702.03573}}</ref> If <math>\Delta X\neq -1</math>, then<math display="block">\mathcal{L}\biggl(\frac{1}{\mathcal{E}(X)}\biggr)_t = X_0-X_t-[X]^c_t
+\sum_{s\leq t}\frac{(\Delta X_s)^2}{1+\Delta X_s}.</math>

== Applications ==

* [[Girsanov theorem|Girsanov's theorem]] can be paraphrased as follows: Let <math>Q</math> be a [[probability measure]] equivalent to another probability measure <math>P</math>. Denote by <math>Z</math> the uniformly integrable martingale closed by <math>Z_\infty = dQ/dP</math>. For a semimartingale <math>U</math> the following are equivalent:
*# Process <math>U</math> is special under <math>Q</math>.
*# Process <math>U+[U,\mathcal{L}(Z)]</math> is special under <math>P</math>.
*+ If either of these conditions holds, then the <math>Q</math>-drift of <math>U</math> equals the <math>P</math>-drift of <math>U+[U,\mathcal{L}(Z)]</math>.
